To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the number of CgA expressing tumours is low; 2) the presence of Cga positive cells in human colonic tumours is not a common event; 3) the presence of these cells in human colons tumours is not related with the differentiation degree of the tumour.
CgA positive elements occur in a small number of human colonic adenomas.

CgA positive tumours are a rare form of colonic adenocarinoma, that they occur more often in the moderately differentiated form, that the CgA positive cell clusters are irregular and diffuse in distribution and that the CgAs positive cells are components of the neoplastic cell population.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the presence of Cgs positive cells in human colonic tumours.
the demonstration of a neuroendocrine differentiation of colonic adenocaricinoma.

the presence of Cga positive cells in a set of 48 cases of moderately differentiated and 7 cases of poorly differentiated human colonic adenomas, and in two cases of well differentiated human colonic carcinomas.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
CgA positive elements in human colonic neoplasms should be considered as an indicator of neuroendocrine differentiation and not as a specific marker of carcinoid tumours.
CgA immunostaining should be performed on all adenocarcinomata to identify a possible neuroendocrine differentiation.
CgA positive cell components are a rare finding in human colonic carcinoma.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the CgA positive tumours could be considered as a particular histotype of adenocarcinomatous differentiation, and the presence of these cells could be considered as an additional prognostic parameter in colonic cancer.

the presence of Cga positive cells in human colonic carcinoma should be taken into account in the histological diagnosis of this neoplastic lesion and, in some cases, the immunohistochemical detection of CgA could represent an important tool for a better definition of the histotype and the prognosis of colonic tumours.
CgA immunohistochemistry should be considered a valuable diagnostic aid in the histological examination of human colorectal adenocarcinomata, in order to detect the presence of neuroendocrine cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that
CgA immunostaining should be considered as an additional diagnostic tool for the evaluation of poorly differentiated colonic adenocarciomas.
the presence of Cga positive cells in colonic adenocarinomas is a rare event and that the use of immunohistochemical techniques may help to establish a correct histological diagnosis.
immunohistochemical staining is necessary in the histological diagnosis of human colonic adenomas and adenocarcinomatous lesions.
